summary: Proposes TCP Port Service Multiplexer (TCPMUX), a way for future TCP services to be reached by name through one port instead of each getting its own well-known port. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 7805.

plainLanguage.summary: TCPMUX lets a client ask for a service by name at one shared TCP port. The server either accepts the request and starts that service or closes the connection.

questions: how does the tcp port service multiplexer work
how does a client choose a tcpmux service
subtitle: A way to select a TCP service by name through one shared port.

tldr.problem: Well-known TCP port numbers are limited, while services may need a way for unknown clients to contact them.
tldr.mechanism: A client connects to TCP port 1 and sends a case-insensitive service name followed by CRLF. A positive reply starts that service's protocol; a negative reply closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1078 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 7805.

today: RFC 1078 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 7805, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: One Port for Multiple Services
sections.content: TCP ports identify the ends of logical connections. Standard TCP services have unique well-known port numbers, which the RFC says were assigned in the range 0 to 255 and were limited in number. TCPMUX offers another way to contact multiple services: clients use a service name at one well-known port rather than needing a separate assigned port for each service.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of choosing a different well-known port for every service, a client can reach a shared port and name the service it wants.

sections.title: Requesting a Service
sections.content: The client connects to the remote host on TCP port 1 and sends the service name followed by a carriage return and line feed. Service names are not case-sensitive. The server replies with a plus sign for a positive acknowledgment or a minus sign for a negative one, optionally followed by an explanation ending in CRLF. After a positive reply, the selected protocol begins; after a negative reply, the connection closes.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends the service name. A plus sign means that service can begin; a minus sign means the connection will close.

sections.title: Service Names
sections.content: The name HELP is reserved. It makes the server return a multi-line list of supported service names and then close the connection. Names listed in the current Assigned Numbers document are reserved for their defined services. For private protocols, the RFC recommends a name likely to be unique, such as one prefixed by an organization name; a protocol version may also be appended.
sections.plainLanguage: HELP asks for the list of services. The RFC recommends distinctive names for private services so clients can tell them apart.
